property_summary: The owner() getter must return the actual owner set during construction, i.e. the deployer address; the buggy version always returns address(0) so it violates that for any caller.
The owner() getter must return the deployer address when called by any party; the buggy version returns address(0), violating the rule for the deployer.

The owner() getter must return the address that was set as owner during construction; the mutant returns address(0) for any caller, so calling owner() on the contract after deployment yields a value different from the original deployer.
Calling owner() on the contract must return a non-zero address; the mutant returns address(0), violating the rule for any caller.
The owner() getter must return the same address for any caller, but the mutant returns address(0) when called by a non-deployer after the deployer renounces ownership.
The owner() function must return the immutable owner set during Ownable construction, not msg.sender; the mutant breaks this by returning the caller instead of the stored owner.

Calling owner() must always return the address that was set as owner during Ownable construction (the deployer), regardless of who calls it; the mutant violates this by returning _msgSender() (the caller) instead of the stored _owner.

Calling owner() must always return the address recorded as owner during Ownable construction regardless of the caller; the mutant returns _msgSender() which changes with the caller, so a non-owner caller will receive its own address instead of the true owner.
Calling owner() must always return the same address for any caller, whereas the mutant returns the caller's address, so two different callers will see different return values.

Calling owner() from two different EOAs must return the same address for both callers; the mutant breaks this by returning the caller's address instead of the stored owner, so two different callers receive different return values.
The owner() function must return the stored _owner address for any caller, but the mutant incorrectly returns tx.origin, breaking the rule when a contract calls owner() on behalf of an EOA.

The owner() function must return the address that was set as owner during construction regardless of who calls it, but the mutant returns tx.origin instead of the stored _owner, violating this when called by a contract acting on behalf of an EOA.

For any caller that is a contract, `c.owner()` must return the same stored owner address, but the mutant returns tx.origin which differs from the stored owner when a contract calls `owner()` on behalf of an EOA.
The owner() function must return _owner regardless of the caller, but the mutant returns tx.origin, so when a contract calls owner() via an EOA, the returned value differs from the stored owner.

owner() must always return the stored _owner set during construction, regardless of caller; the buggy version returns tx.origin, so when any contract calls owner() on behalf of an EOA, the returned address differs from the true owner.

For any caller, after transferOwnership(newOwner) completes, the owner() must never be address(0). The bug removes the zero-address check, so a call with newOwner = address(0) sets owner to zero, breaking the invariant.
After any call to transferOwnership, owner() must return a non-zero address. The bug removes the zero-address check, so a call with newOwner = address(0) sets owner to zero, breaking the invariant.
For any call to transferOwnership, the owner() must remain non-zero; the bug allows address(0) to become owner because the zero-address require was removed.
After any call to transferOwnership, the owner must be either the previous owner or the new owner; the bug allows setting owner to address(0), making owner() return address(0) which is neither.
After any call to transferOwnership, the owner() must remain a non-zero address; the bug removes the zero-address check, allowing address(0) to be set as the new owner.
After transferOwnership is called with a valid non-zero address, the owner() of the contract should equal that address; the buggy version sets owner to address(0) regardless of the newOwner passed.
After a call to transferOwnership(newOwner) where newOwner is a non-zero address that is not the current owner, the owner() must equal newOwner; the mutant always sets owner to address(0) instead.
After transferOwnership(newOwner) with newOwner != address(0) and msg.sender == current owner, owner() must equal newOwner; the mutant always sets owner to address(0).

After any call to transferOwnership with a non-zero newOwner that does not revert, owner() must return a non-zero address; the buggy implementation always sets the owner to address(0), violating this invariant.
For any non-zero newOwner, after a successful transferOwnership(newOwner) by the current owner, owner() must not equal address(0); the mutant breaks this by always setting the owner to address(0).
Only the current owner (as returned by c.owner()) can successfully change the owner via transferOwnership; removing the onlyOwner modifier allows any caller to do so.
For any address that is not the current owner of C, calling transferOwnership will revert in the reference but succeed in the mutant.
For any caller that is not the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) succeeds in the mutant but must revert in the reference.

For ANY caller (including non-owner), calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the reference C must revert when newOwner is non-zero and the caller is not the current owner, but succeeds in the mutant which removed the onlyOwner modifier.
For any caller who is not the current owner, transferOwnership(newOwner) must revert in the reference contract, but succeeds in the mutant.
The name() function must always return the string "DCF Token" as set in the constructor; the buggy version returns "DifferentName", violating this invariant.

The name() function must return the same string as set in the ERC20 constructor; the buggy version always returns "DifferentName" regardless of constructor argument, so calling name() yields a different result than the name passed to the constructor.

The name() function must return the value of the internal _name variable set during construction. The buggy version returns a hardcoded string "DifferentName", breaking the invariant that name() matches the constructor argument.

The name() function must return the same string for the entire lifetime of the contract; the buggy version returns 'DifferentName' regardless of original name, while the reference always returns the immutable constructor argument.

For any initial ownership and any caller, the name() function must return the string that was passed as the first argument to the constructor of ERC20; the buggy version always returns 'DifferentName', so it fails to satisfy this relation for the actual constructor argument 'DCF Token'.
For any input, calling the public view function name() on the ERC20 token C must match the string passed to the constructor ("DCF Token"); the bug returns an empty string.
For any caller, the public view function name() on the ERC20 token C must return the exact string passed to the ERC20 constructor ("DCF Token"), but the buggy version returns an empty string.
For any caller, calling the public view function name() on the ERC20 token C must return the exact string passed to the ERC20 constructor ("DCF Token"), but the buggy version returns an empty string.
For any caller, the public view function name() on the ERC20 token C must return a non-empty string; the buggy version returns an empty string, violating this universal property.
For any caller, the public view function name() on the ERC20 token C must return the exact string passed to the ERC20 constructor ("DCF Token"), but the buggy version returns an empty string.
For any caller, calling name() returns exactly the string passed to the constructor; the bug appends 'X', so the returned string differs from the original name.

The result of calling name() on C must start with the original name and its length must be exactly the length of the original name; the buggy version appends 'X' making the returned string longer than the original name, violating the length equality.

The name() function must return a string that does not end with 'X' (using the last byte of the result), which the reference version satisfies for any initial name, but the buggy version appends 'X' and thus the returned string ends with 'X'.
The name() function should return a non-empty string; the buggy version appends 'X', so for an empty initial name the return becomes non-empty, violating that the original empty name remains empty.

The name() function must return a string whose bytes32 representation is equal to the bytes32 representation of the original _name; the bug appends 'X', making the bytes32 conversion different for some original names.
Calling symbol() on any valid ERC20 token must return its stored symbol string, but the buggy version always returns the hardcoded string "DIFF" instead.
For any address that is not a whitelisted or blacklisted account, the symbol() getter returns exactly the string that was passed to the constructor; the buggy version returns "DIFF" instead.
The reference contract's symbol() must return the string "DCF" set in the constructor, but the buggy version hardcodes "DIFF", so for any input the values differ.

For any allowed caller, the public view getter `symbol()` must return the string that was originally set in the constructor, but the buggy version always returns a different hardcoded string, violating this rule for all callers.
For any caller, c.symbol() must return the string 'DCF' set in the constructor, but the buggy version always returns 'DIFF'.
The decimals() function of the reference contract returns 18, while the buggy version returns 8; thus if any external contract relies on the expected number of decimals the invariant is violated.
The decimals() function must always return 18, matching the standard ERC20 token definition; the buggy version returns 8, breaking this invariant.
The reference C.decimals() always returns 18; the buggy version returns 8, violating the invariant that the return value equals 18.
The `decimals()` function must return 18 as expected by the UniswapV2Pair during initialization, which the buggy version violates by returning 8.
The decimals() function must return exactly 18; the buggy version returns 8, violating this invariant for any call.
The decimals() function must return 18; the buggy version returns 0, violating the expected ERC20 metadata.
The decimals() function must return 18, the standard ERC20 decimal places, for any caller; the buggy version returns 0, violating that invariant.
For any caller, `c.decimals()` must return exactly 18 (the reference standard), whereas the buggy version returns 0, breaking the immutable metadata invariant.
For any caller, c.decimals() must return the same immutable value defined at construction (18), but the bug returns 0.
For any caller, c.decimals() must return exactly 18 as specified by the ERC20 implementation, but the buggy version returns 0.
The decimals() function of the reference contract always returns 18, whereas the buggy version returns 6, so for any fuzzed input the return values will differ.

A call to decimals() on any valid instance of C always returns 18 in the reference, but the buggy version returns 6 for the same call, violating the invariant that the return value is exactly the expected constant for that contract.
The decimals() function should return 18, the standard for typical ERC20 tokens, but the buggy version returns 6.

The `decimals()` view function always returns the same value for every call to a given contract instance; the reference returns 18 and the buggy one returns 6, so the rule 'decimals() equals the initial value observed' holds for the reference but fails for the mutant.
The decimals() function must return 18 when queried through the ERC20Metadata interface that C inherits, but the buggy version returns 6 instead.

The totalSupply() function must return the sum of all minted tokens minus all burned tokens (initial mint of 2000000e18), which the reference satisfies and the mutant violates by returning a hardcoded 1000000e18.

The totalSupply() must equal the initial mint amount (2000000e18) minus any tokens burned later, which the reference satisfies but the mutant always returns 1000000e18, so any burn via transfer to the pair makes the reference return less than 2000000e18 while the mutant stays at 1000000e18.

After minting 2000000e18 tokens, totalSupply() must equal the actual internal totalSupply accounting (initial mint minus any tokens burned later); the mutant always returns a hardcoded 1000000e18, so any burn makes the reference totalSupply less than the original mint but the mutant still returns 1000000e18 instead of tracking the real supply.

The totalSupply() must equal the internal actual supply (initial 2000000e18 minus any burned tokens), which the reference satisfies but the mutant violates by returning a hardcoded 1000000e18, causing any burn to make the reference totalSupply less than 2000000e18 while the mutant still returns 1000000e18.
For any total supply modifications (mint, burn, transfer to pair that triggers burnPair), reference totalSupply tracks actual supply while mutant always returns hardcoded 1000000e18.
The totalSupply function must return the exact sum of all minted and burned tokens, but the mutant always returns _totalSupply - 1, breaking this invariant for any initial supply.
The totalSupply() function must return the exact _totalSupply value, but the mutant always returns _totalSupply - 1, so for any initial mint the two values differ.
